title: Beyond Precipitation Deficit: Driver‐Based Classification of Hydrological Droughts in an Alpine Basin
content:
Abstract

Hydrological droughts in mountain basins can arise from different combinations of precipitation deficits, snow accumulation and melt anomalies, and seasonal storage conditions. Here, we develop a deterministic, locally calibrated framework to classify recurrent hydro-meteorological pathways associated with streamflow drought onset in the Upper Adige basin, Italy. The framework combines simulated precipitation, temperature, snow water equivalent (SWE), snowmelt, and streamflow with seasonal information in a rule-based decision tree. Applied to 743 drought events across 22 sub-basins over 1992–2023, the classification identifies distinct drought types with different duration, intensity, severity, and seasonal signatures. Composite droughts are the most frequent (26.8%), while warm and cold snow season pathways together account for 33.0% of events. Rain-to-snow droughts have the longest median duration and highest median severity, whereas warm snow season droughts show the highest median intensity. Sensitivity analyses show that the broad classification structure is retained across alternative design choices, although some decision parameters exert a strong control on class allocation and require local calibration. Hydro-meteorological anomalies also provide season- and lead-time-dependent information on subsequent drought occurrence: spring SWE deficits and autumn precipitation deficits (mostly in October) were linked with the larger increase in drought probability. Our proposed framework provides a transparent basis for characterizing and tracking distinct drought-onset pathways in mountain catchments and for informing process-based drought monitoring.
